title: Estimating and Testing Long-Run Risk Models: International Evidence
abstract: We estimate and test long-run risk models using international macroeconomic and financial data. The benchmark model features a representative agent who has recursive preferences with a time preference shock, a persistent component in expected consumption growth, and stochastic volatility in fundamentals characterized by an autoregressive Gamma process. We construct a comprehensive dataset with quarterly frequency in the post-war period for ten developed countries and employ an efficient likelihood-based Bayesian method that exploits up-to-date sequential Monte Carlo methods to make full econometric inference. Our estimation provides international evidence in support of long-run risks, time-varying preference shocks, and countercyclicality of the stochastic discount factor.
summary_en: Most long-run risk evidence comes from US data alone, leaving open the question of whether the model's preference parameters and volatility processes are stable across countries. The authors estimate a long-run risk model — featuring recursive preferences with time-preference shocks, persistent expected consumption growth, and autoregressive-gamma stochastic volatility — on quarterly post-war data from ten developed countries. The international evidence supports the existence of long-run risks, time-varying preference shocks, and a countercyclical stochastic discount factor, broadly aligning with US-only findings while exposing meaningful cross-country differences in preference parameters.
data_used: Quarterly post-war consumption growth, equity returns, risk-free rates and price-dividend ratios for ten developed countries (US, UK, Canada, Australia, Japan, Germany, France, Italy, Switzerland, Netherlands), assembled from OECD, national statistical offices and Datastream.
policy_relevance: International long-run risk evidence informs sovereign wealth fund and pension-fund return assumptions outside the US. The paper provides cross-country preference-parameter estimates useful for institutions whose liabilities are not denominated in dollars — including Hungary's State Treasury and pension funds — when calibrating long-horizon discount rates and stress scenarios.
